```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#install.packages("funFEM")
library(funFEM)
data(velib)
data = velib$data
dim(data)
```
we have 181 variables and 1189 observations. Each observation is the loading profile of a station and each column is a time point. 
```{r}
names(data)
```
```{r}
pairs(data[,1:5])
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

idx <- sample(nrow(data), 100)

matplot(
  t(data[idx, ]),
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  col = rgb(0, 0, 0, alpha = 0.3),
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = "Value"
)
```

```{r}
pc = princomp(data)
summary(pc)
```

If we apply the rule of the 90%, with d = 20 we already have about 90% of the full variance.
```{r}
screeplot(pc,npcs=30)
```
if we apply the elbow rule we can use just the first 5 components. 

# Hierarchical Clustering  

```{r}
plot(hclust(dist(data),method = "single"))
plot(hclust(dist(data),method = "complete"))
plot(hclust(dist(data),method = "centroid"))
plot(hclust(dist(data),method = "ward.D2"))
```
we can chose complete linkage or ward distance because the tree seems balance.  
```{r}
#complete 
hc = hclust(dist(data),method = "complete")
plot(hc)
```

we need to cut the tree at branch that is the largest jumpe which k =3

```{r}
plot(hc)
rect.hclust(hc,k = 3)
```
```{r}
w_hc = hclust(dist(data),method = "ward.D2")
plot(w_hc)
```
we choose k = 4 for ward distance
```{r}
plot(w_hc)
rect.hclust(w_hc,k = 4)
```

```{r}
X = as.matrix(data,ncol = ncol(data))

# perform PCA, then project the data on the new PCA system, take the first 2 principle components 
X.2d = predict(princomp(X))[,1:2]

hc = hclust(dist(data),method = "complete")
clust = cutree(hc,k = 3)
#plot the cluster with the compete method result on the 2 pca components 
plot(X.2d,col=clust,pch=19)
```

```{r}
w_hc = hclust(dist(data),method = "ward.D2")
w_clust = cutree(w_hc,k =4 )
#plot the cluster with the compete method result on the 2 pca components 
plot(X.2d,col=w_clust,pch=19)
```
```{r}
set.seed(123)

idx <- sample(nrow(data), 20)

matplot(
  t(data[idx, ]),
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  col = clust,
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = "Value"
)
```

# K-means
find the best k for kmeans using criterions $$J(K) = \frac{B(K)}{S}$$
```{r}
K.max = 20
J = rep(NA,K.max)
for (k in 1:K.max){
  out = kmeans(data, centers = k, nstart = 10)
  J[k] = out$betweenss / out$totss
}
plot(1:K.max,J,type='b',col='blue')
lines(1:K.max,J,type='s',lty=3,col='gray')

```
from this plot we can take K = 4 or 5. in order to compare with the previous reslut i take k=4
```{r}
km = kmeans(data, centers = 4, nstart = 10)
plot(X.2d,col=km$cluster,pch=19)
```
```{r}
set.seed(123)

idx <- sample(nrow(data), 20)

matplot(
  t(data[idx, ]),
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  col = km$cluster,
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = "Value"
)
```

From the result projected on the first 2 component of PCA, it seems that K-Mean can separate the data better. 
```{r}

matplot(
  t(km$centers),
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  xlab = "Time",
  ylab = "Value"
)
```
Among all the 1189 stations we can cluster them into 4 groups that have similar behavior over time
